utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to our technicians, our interpreters, legal assistants, court reporters; good morning, Madam Registrar; good morning, Mr. Harmon, Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Cayley; good morning, Mr. Petrusic and Mr. Visnjic; good morning, General Krstic. We will resume with our work today. Mr. McCloskey will continue examining the witness. I think that Mr. Petrusic was not nervous yesterday. We're all doing our job here. We will be working until 3.00 today so that we can finish with the examination-in-chief. Let me propose a schedule for today. We will have three breaks during our working day today. We will be working from half past nine until 11.00. At 11.00 we will have a 20-minute break. Then we will be working from 11.20 until 12.50, which will be followed by a half-hour break. Then after that, there will be a working period from 1.00 [as interpreted] until ten minutes past two, and then we'll have a half-hour break and work until the end, that is, until 3.00. I will not interrupt you, but this is a tentative schedule for today. Good morning, Mr. Butler. You will continue answering questions that will be put to you by Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. McCloskey: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We left off yesterday going over some intercepts from 17 July. I'd like to take us back in time for one document that I inadvertently bypassed yesterday and that's taking us back to 15 July, to Exhibit 596A. It may be in another binder, but Mr. Butler has got it and can get it on the ELMO. Mr. Butler, can you explain to us what this document is, who it's to, what its relevance is to your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an intelligence report from the intelligence organ of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade to the command of the Drina Corps, dated 15 July 1995. What this document is and what it represents is the understanding of Captain First Class Dusko Vukotic, the Chief of Intelligence of the Zvornik Brigade, pertaining to the situation with the column that is penetrating the rear zone of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. If you will remember back to the 15 July 1995 interim report written by Colonel Pandurevic, much of the enemy information that's described in this report is incorporated in that interim report to the Corps as well. If I can direct your attention to the second paragraph, this is for the first time where the idea is surfaced that the Corps should give some consideration to the effects and consequences of opening a corridor for the armed head of the column, letting them through, and then closing it and dealing with the remainder of the column in the Corps' zone -- in the Zvornik Brigade zone, sorry. As you can tell by this message and the date stamp underneath, it was sent out at approximately 1213 hours on 15 July, so it arrived at the Corps -- was sent to the Corps approximately four hours prior to the interim combat report by Colonel Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this reflects the actual deal that Colonel Pandurevic did the next day with the Muslim column.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on, then, back to where we left off yesterday. It should be Exhibit 662A, an intercept of 17 July, 1244 hours. What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular intercept between an X subscriber, who's unidentified, and Trbic of the Zvornik Brigade discusses X looking for Pop, or Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, the Assistant Commander for Security of the Zvornik Brigade. Further down it notes that they're to leave right away for here, "for Zlatar 01," he says. Zlatar 01, as we've previously discussed, being the designator for the Commander of the Drina Corps, General Krstic. He notes that -- in this case, Captain Trbic notes that it's difficult for him to get in touch with him. "... it's very hard for me to do that" from where they're located. The rest of the conversation, the reflection of the fact that he'll do what he can and try and get in touch with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what task do you think they're talking about that Pop is involved in north of Trbic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Working under the assumption that Trbic is, in fact, at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters in Karakaj, in Zvornik, the only tasks north on the 17th would be those related to the burial of bodies which occurs at the Branjevo Military Farm on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to the next exhibit, 664A, just a few minutes after this conversation that we've just spoke of, at 1249 hours on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular conversation, again, between an unidentified subscriber and Trbic, the discussion that the guidance has changed. "Let him" continue to "finish that work." Presumably we're talking about that same "him" being Lieutenant Colonel Popovic. And then once he's done, "have him report immediately here at (Golac's?)" The closest that I infer from that is that they're referring to Golic, which in that case would make it Zlatar headquarters, to Major Golic, or where he's located. Trbic is confirming that he will let him continue his work, he won't disturb him, and then he'll tell him when he stops back here at Palma.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The comment by Trbic, "The preparation is mainly finished," what do you take that for?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that in that particular instance what they're talking about is the work related to burying the bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit 666A, 17 July, 1622 hours; Popovic on one side of a conversation and Y who is inaudible. What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, Popovic reporting back to somebody that he sees as a superior figure, or it's inferred by him. Letting whomever that is know that the job is done; it's all completed. Letting him know he's at the base. In that respect, the base I believe he's talking from is the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade. The last line is letting it know that the job gets an A, a grade A, that everything is done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little mystery line at the bottom. "French is heard in the background." You don't know anything about that, I take it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot explain that at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why they're speaking French in the Zvornik Brigade. All right. Let's go to Exhibit 668A, 17 July, 1850 hours. Could you just tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a rather long one. If I could just go through some of the names. Participants: Mirko and X, X being unidentified. Mirko, I believe, is Lieutenant Mirko Petrovic who is a Drina Corps officer who's in charge of intercepting communications from -- I'm sorry, a Zvornik Brigade officer who intercepts communications from the Muslim radio operators. He identifies first Jevtevic, which is Major Jevtevic of the Drina Corps, the Commander of the 5th Communications Battalion. What the context of the discussion pertains to is the fact that an individual has been identified, a Muslim individual, who was the chief radio operator or signalsman for Naser Oric, and it notes that he is in the custody of the Zvornik Brigade. They identify the individual of -- they identify him as Ibraham Becirovic. He notes that he received that information from a "Colonel Stankovic" who "was in Zvornik today." As we've previously noted and we've seen on that 17 July Main Staff order, Colonel Stankovic is a member of the VRS Main Staff. He further notes that what they want to do is, because this is a high-value individual, that they want to get him and they want to interrogate him, and as such they want to try and call this guy up because of his intelligence value. They also note, rather snidely, at the bottom of this that Colonel Stankovic doesn't know the identity of the man he's talked to, so they're going through some work trying to figure out who knows that Becirovic is in the custody of the Zvornik Brigade. Turning to the second page of the intercept, again, more reflection that it's a notation that he is among one of them in the middle of the column where they asked, "So he is over there among the prisoners?" An acknowledgment by Mirko that the Zvornik Brigade does have a considerable number of prisoners or at least some prisoners. Further down, talking about, "We'll finish off that job. Because I'd say he probably knows a great deal more about the 2nd Corps and the Main Staff ..." I believe here we're talking about the BiH Main Staff then, "than Tursun or Naser, and probably about the educated people and others."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you go on to the next page, I just want to point out one sentence in the middle. It says, "Go on, go and look for him and check with him at home if he is anywhere so we can find him before some mafia picks him up and kills him there and other things before I finish this job." What do you think that is a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is a reference to the understanding that at least X is aware that prisoners are being killed in the zone of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But by 17 July, most of the of the organised executions, as we know of them, have been finished already by the 16th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. In this instance, we also know from documents that, for the most part, Muslims who were taken prisoner from the column were also executed in small groupings and as we get into additional exhibits further down the line, we will demonstrate that. But again, the awareness of the fact that for the most part, prisoners who are captured from the column by the Zvornik Brigade on the 15th, 16th 17th and 18th, they are being executed shortly after their capture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you have anything else in that one?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last line just concludes the conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go on to 671A, a conversation at 1950 hours, the participants: "Krstic - X - Commander (MLADIC)." What do you make of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This, I believe, is related to Zepa. A discussion between the Corps Commander, General Krstic on the 17th and General Mladic noting that General Mladic is not accepting the conditions relative to negotiations at Zepa and that General Krstic is to continue military operations. Further, he notes that he wants General Krstic to get in touch with Miletic who is General Major Miletic the Chief of Operations of the Main Staff where presumably, General Miletic has additional instructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They're talking about the Turks' conditions. Now, we've heard a lot of deals and things about the Srebrenica/Zvornik area. Can you tell us what you believe this is related to, what is the conditions in the Zepa area, what are the conditions or what is that about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, not being deeply versed in the activities relative to the political situation in Zepa, what I believe that we're discussing here is the issue pertaining to how Mladic was looking for the unconditional surrender of the forces there, and how the BiH government did not want to give up the enclave and was specifically ordering the military forces in Zepa not to surrender to the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And up a little further in the conversation, General Mladic appears to be referring to General Krstic as "Krle". Is that the same Krle we heard on the videotape when Mladic and General Krstic came into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's a nickname for General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I also noted that General Mladic wants Krstic to get in touch with Miletic on the secure line. Now, we've had a lot intercepts where we see people speaking in open and sometimes in vague terms. Can you tell us what you know, if anything, about their -- General Krstic's and the brigade's ability to communicate in a secure means at this time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Understanding the communications network that the VRS possessed at the time, the standard open telephone network, the radio telephone network that they had that was designed to operate in secure voice mode, and in many cases was unable to do so because there were technical problems. So primarily while it was designed to operate in a secure voice mode, it did not do so, and most of the intercepts that we discussed come off of that voice network that is being spoken, as we say, in the open or in the clear. We understand, particularly in the case of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, that during the period, their voice encryption devices were not operating and as a result, their only voice mechanism was, for the most, part unsecure. The other method that the brigades and other elements could communicate through was the radio and teletype messages that we've displayed prior in testimony. Those messages go over a secure data network and as such are considered secure because the BiH side did not have the technology necessary to decipher those communications. So while in many respects it was understood that the BiH could and did listen to the non-secure voice communications, it was also understood that the BiH did not have the capability to decipher and intercept the radio teletype communications. Consequently, those were known to be the most secure means of communication and the most sensitive traffic went over those means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just in passing, what value, then, would you give to the unsecure communications if they had the secure means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one disadvantage that you have with the secure means of communications, and as we've noted in previous testimony, the penalty that is paid is the penalty of time. It takes time to write out the message, and in some cases, it takes several hours from when the message is actually written to when the message is actually transmitted. So in many cases, with very time-sensitive information, commanders opted to use the unsecure voice network because the timeliness of the information was perceived to be more important than the risk if the Bosnian Muslims intercepted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it is a must sometimes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that we had some communications like that. Were you meaning we had BiH communications or VRS communications? What did you mean by that when you are referring to "we had examples of secure communications"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: An example of the secure communications would be the daily and interim combat reports from the brigades to the Corps. Those are formalised written reports. They are sent over the secure radio teletype network, sent to the Corps headquarters. Those are the types of reports that I'm referring to that are sent over the secure communications means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we received those combat reports through the search warrant at the various brigades and not by -- not by the BiH actually capturing them over the airwaves; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. All of the reports of that nature we obtained through seizures. No information pertaining to those reports could have been collected by the BiH government over the airwaves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to Exhibit 673A, later in the day, 2026 hours. This appears to be a reference to Pop and that he has gone home at this point and is in no mood for some reason. So let's go on to Exhibit 675A which now takes us into 18 July, and we've started off with the interim combat report for that date. And can you, again, give us the highlights of this report, what we can glean from it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report, again, an interim combat report discussing the significant situation in the Zvornik Brigade. For the most part, it's noting that the brigade is active in operations rounding up the remaining formations from the column that are in the territory. Paragraph two, the Brigade Commander rolls up or notes what his forces are at that time, noting that his forces include a company from the Krajina 16th Brigade, a company of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, two platoons of the Bijeljina Military Police, and one platoon from the Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade. So in that respect, he's reflecting that all of those forces are, in fact, under his command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How does that work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces in question as they come into his zone and are put under his command are essentially for the period of time resubordinated to him. In the case of the forces that come from the Drina Corps, for example, the company from the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, the Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade forces, those would have been directed into a zone by the Corps Command and then placed under his command for the duration that they are there. You'll note there are formations from well outside of the Corps zone. A company from the Krajina Corps, the 1st Krajina Corps and from the Bijeljina Military Police, those from the East Bosnia Corps. In those instances for those units, they would have had to have been made available to the Drina Corps first by the Main Staff in order to go into the Corps zone by the Main Staff. And then, at that point, what would have happened is they would have come under the control of the Drina Corps who would have further given them to the control and -- command and control of the Zvornik Brigade Commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It also notes that he has no reserves despite this additional help. So that is a difficult situation still.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I note just below that the R, or perhaps, Reserve Battalion has been mobilised and is involved in sealing off and searching. Wasn't the person that was driving the truck to the Pilica cultural centre on the day before, on the 17th from the R Battalion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the R Battalion, the day before was doing something else.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And I would also draw your attention to the last line of point two where it says, "The brigade will continue to inspect the territory of Zone 1," listing various names including "Petkovci-Baljkovica-Memici front line." Those three words will become relevant in an intercept. Can you explain why that will be so we don't have to come back to this report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially, as one would expect, this report going up to the Drina Corps Command, they are getting their information, the Drina Corps Command is receiving their information from this report. And in the form of one of the later intercepts that we have, there was some question pertaining to where this line ran. Somebody at the Drina Corps was updating a map and their graphics and had called down to the Zvornik Brigade referencing this report to discuss where this line specifically ran.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we have a list of casualties up to that point for the Srebrenica and Zepa operations.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What this listing does is it encompasses three lists: The casualties recently incurred, the casualties from March of 1995 through the beginning of Krivaja 95, and then a composite roll-up of the all of the casualties pertaining to the first six months of 1995, noting that out of an end strength of approximately 4.000 or so troops, 479 total casualties were taken by the brigade in six months, almost ten per cent. And this casualty roll-up sets the stage for a series of very critical observations that come down in paragraph four pertaining to what the brigade is being used for and why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that second page, just below the numbers, the writer of this report is directing the attention to the Corps -- "I would direct the Corps Command's attention to these alarming figures," so the author is speaking to the Corps Command not the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How does that fit in with the theory that the Main Staff is the one that is in charge of the Zvornik Brigade and is running the show in that regard?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't fit into that theory at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These casualties figures, is it possible that they could have been reduced had the Drina Corps assets used for slaughtering Muslim prisoners and guarding Muslim prisoners, if those had been put in the front line, is it possible that these casualty figures may have been reduced?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the size and intensity of the combat and just the sheer size of the column, it's possible that they would have been reduced by a little bit. It would have meant an additional, perhaps, 50 to 100 combatants that could have been involved in the combat operations. That part I can say with some certainty, that it would have brought more to the battle, but I'm not sure that I could speculate as to whether or not another 100 combatants would have affected the casualty rates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You referred to paragraph 4 earlier. What do you get from paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 4 represents for the first time a number that the VRS itself establishes for the number of military-aged Muslim men that were at one time stored in schools in the zone of the Zvornik municipality. Again, the writer of the report -- I believe the writer of the report is, in fact, Colonel Pandurevic in this case -- is noting that over the last ten days, the municipality has been swamped with Srebrenica Turks, and to him it is inconceivable that somebody brought 3.000 Turks of military age and placed them in schools in the municipality, in addition to the 7.000 or so who fled into the forests. So very specifically here, Colonel Pandurevic is differentiating between the Muslims who were part of the column and the Muslim military-aged men who were in the schools at the time. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French an English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can I just ask you one question about that figure that bothered me. Most of the information that we've gotten so far has suggested that the number of military-aged men who came up from Potocari, didn't come up through the column but came up through Potocari, was much smaller than this. I never heard this big a figure as opposed to what we heard, the 7.000 or 8.000 or more in the column. I'm just wandering if that scores with -- that's much larger than the figure I remember of military-aged men who were bused out of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In looking at this number, and this is their hard number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the only way to really go back and look at that number is trying to generate a series of numbers from those that were killed at the execution sites and how many were being held at the schools. I believe that the rough figures that the investigation has generated is somewhere at approximately 1.000 at Orahovac, perhaps 800 to 1.000 at Petkovci, and several thousand up in the Pilica area between the Dom Kulture, the school, and a completely unknown number who may have been held at the school at Rocevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My understanding was those were composite groups; that a lot of the people taken off who surrendered from the column or were captured from the column were then marched off into these schools, or at least that's the kind of testimony that we've been getting. So that the school number represented a combination of some from Potocari, but primarily people came off of the column. So the phraseology that he used, "Somebody brought in 3.000 Turks and placed them in the schools in addition to the 7.000 who have fled into the forest," and you remarked on the differentiation made between the two groups. That's what confused me. Because my understanding from previous testimony was that the people in the schools or on the killing fields, et cetera, a lot of those were people who were out of the columns.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where I believe he is differentiating here is, the column breakup, as he understands it, in the zone, we know that the people who were taken from the column in the zone of Bratunac got incorporated in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade was not incorporating or not taking anyone out of the column as it went into the zone of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So Colonel Pandurevic has only two frames of reference: those prisoners that he received from Bratunac, which encompasses those including the column down there, and the column, which is a separate one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. That makes sense. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, let me ask you a bit again about this 3.000 number that Colonel Pandurevic uses as military men placed in his schools. Now, I want to go back to the 15 July conversation where Beara says he has 3.500 parcels to distribute, and we know at the time of that conversation, the people at Orahovac and the people at Petkovci have all been murdered or killed. So in that sense, how do you, if you can, analyse Colonel Beara's number of having 3.500 people still left on the afternoon of the 15th to deal with, and Colonel Pandurevic's number which appears to be a total number of 3.000 for the schools?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that particular case, it's hard to reconcile the two numbers. I can only speculate that perhaps Colonel Pandurevic didn't count the numbers from the schools at Orahovac and Petkovci, those who were already dead when he returned back into the zone. But that's only speculation on my part. I really can't explain the low figure that Colonel Pandurevic gives and the higher figure that Colonel Beara gives; there is a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, for the Court's information, the exhumation figures, the various figures, we will provide in argument for you to help deal with these various numbers and the situations there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Anything else on this particular interim combat report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The final series is, again looking at paragraph 7, a very pointed request to the Corps to examine and review how their brigade is used, and for future assignments, that they want to be very involved in the process. Again, in its entirety, this is a rather critical report leading me to believe that the only person in the Zvornik Brigade who would author such a report, both in content and in tone, to the Corps Command would be the Brigade Commander personally. I couldn't ascribe this report as being done by either a deputy or a duty officer in that regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we could go on to the next document, Exhibit 676. This is just the regular report for the same day, the 18th. It seems to reflect similar things, just less detail. Do you have anything to say on this report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Just the based premise that, again, this report is going to the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then let's get on to the intercepts of 18 July, starting with Exhibit 677A, 0712 hours. Can you tell us briefly how this fits into your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This intercept is a specific conversation between General Major Krstic and Colonel Veletic. As we discussed earlier, Colonel Veletic, normally the Chief of Artillery of the Drina Corps, is in this regard the Commander of the temporary formation which was established, the 4th Drinski Brigade, operating in the zone of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. What I infer or what I get from this message is just, again, a notification or an instance where General Krstic is communicating with other individuals pertaining to issues, in this case, outside the Corps zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit 680A, 0716 hours, the 18th. Tell us about this.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The primary correspondents are General Krstic and Colonel Cerovic, who previously was identified as the Assistant Commander for Moral, Legal, and Religious Affairs of the Drina Corps. Discussing -- first of all, making sure that he's put through to extension 385, and as we've noted earlier on several occasions, the 385 extension drop leads directly to General Krstic. In this particular case, General Krstic is directing Colonel Cerovic to go to a certain location, and I believe that this location is the 1st Birac Brigade, and take command of "that part," that being an unspecified part. He notes other personalities: Lazic and Vlacic. I believe in this context, Lazic is Colonel Milenko Lazic, an operations officer from the Drina Corps, and as we've previously noted, Lieutenant Colonel Vlacic is the Chief of Staff of the Birac Brigade. You can't see it on the ELMO, but at the bottom, a particular notation, a verbal order from General Krstic to Colonel Cerovic letting him know that when Colonel Cerovic gets there, he is to take charge, and reiterating, "so you command." Colonel Cerovic reports back that he "spoke to Vinko last night." He'll send an additional report today; that report being the interim combat report of the 18th July which we've just reviewed. He's letting General Krstic know that he's stabilised the situation. At the bottom, again, General Krstic noting that he expects Colonel Cerovic to restore order there and command. Cerovic acknowledges that order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these the normal actions of a commander in this situation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These represent the normal actions of a corps commander, absolutely. He's keeping -- not only is he keeping fully advised of the situation within his own corps zone, he's going the additional step and designating -- because he perceives a problem with a specific unit or a specific situation, he's designated one of his own assistant commanders to go up there, take command of the issue and to deal with it. So he certainly has an awareness of what's going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's not Zepa.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe we're talking about Zepa here, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go briefly to Exhibit 681A, a 0729 hours conversation. What can you tell us, if anything, about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one conversation is X, the other one is identified as Cero, which may be a nickname for Colonel Cerovic. It notes, "Miljanovic was supposed to go down there too." There are several people who fall into that -- who that name could be so I don't want to speculate. But the reference down towards the end under X, "Well, somewhere in that part. Pop and I were in charge over here in this part," a reference, again, to the slang of Popovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to the next exhibit, 684A, 18 July, a conversation at 1245 hours between B and X, which is -- do you know who these people are, and can you tell us what they're talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context, I'm not able to identify B and X, other than to be able to say that whoever they are, at this particular time, they were rather informed individuals. What I use this particular intercept for is what I call an awareness piece, to show that a lot of individuals have a general awareness of what has been happening in East Bosnia over the past several days. In this context, they're certainly talking about the issue of men from Srebrenica. They identify the situation in Zepa. They note Savcic, who in this regard is Colonel Milomar Savcic, the Commander of the 65th Protection Regiment, whose forces were deployed in the area of Savcic [sic]. They note what was happening with the column, that Pandurevic had to let them pass because he couldn't kill them all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you, Mr. Butler. I think we may need to correct the transcript. It says: "... the 65th Protection Regiment who were deployed in Savcic," but that's not correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. They were deployed near Zepa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They note further down in the conversation a fierce attack in the zone of the 2nd Romanija -- the 2nd Romanija Brigade of the Drina Corps and their zone at Olovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, just primarily the fact that the subscribers are aware or very knowledgable about what's happening in the zone of the entire Drina Corps headquarters or the entire Drina Corps zone. Olovo is, in fact, part of the Drina Corps zone under the control of the 2nd Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Before you go on, let me take you back to the first page. X says they had close to 10.000 men of military age in Srebrenica. The next question is: "Have they reduced them by half?" and the next says, "Well, it must be close to half. 4,000 to 5,000 have certainly kicked the bucket." Now, of course, this term in English "kick the bucket" is a slang term for having died. It's not a literal translation of the B/C/S, but the B/C/S, I'm sure, means the same thing, and I have no idea how that would have been translated into French. But "kick the bucket," in your view, means people who have died; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does that number, 4.000 to 5.000 having died, connect at all to the investigation in your analysis as you've reviewed the investigation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can certainly note that in the case of 4.000 to 5.000, that those numbers would be high if they were only discussing the combat involving the column going through the zone of the Zvornik Brigade because certainly there were nowhere near 4.000 to 5.000 killed in that column in the combat between the 14th and the 17th or 18th of July. I can only speculate that that 4.000 to 5.000 has to include the Muslim men who were taken up and executed in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then on page two, in the middle of the page, X says, "Yeah, Pandurevic had to let them pass because he couldn't kill them all. They surged at them. He lost men. He was afraid that they would break through his line from the other side, you know, because they are close to the line and they attacked from over there." Now, how close does this description match what you know from the daily combat reports and from the other information about Pandurevic opening up the corridor temporarily?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is, in fact, an accurate description.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then why don't you continue on with your analysis.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A series of names that come out talking about who was injured, one name that we understand or that we at least believe we can identify is in the case of Basevic, who was in fact Naser Basevic, the Chief of Technical Services for the Drina Corps. It discusses further down the situation, as they understand it, at Zepa. And in a reflection at the very bottom, one of the very early issues that was brought up and that we saw reflected in the supreme command and Main Staff documents directive number 7 and Main Staff Order 7/1, the recognition that how many units are being tied down or were previously tied down as a result of those enclaves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is that a roughly correct figure, three to four brigades?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of the enclave at Srebrenica, it tied down the entire Bratunac Brigade, the Milici Brigade, elements of the Skelani Separate Battalion. In the case of Zepa, it tied down the Visegrad Brigade and the Rogatica Brigade. In the case of the enclave at Zepa, that tied down additional Drina Corps assets. So that actually may be a low figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anything else to say about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the participants in the last line perceived the International Community as interfering with them. All right. Let's go to the next exhibit, 685A, and I would just direct the Court down to line five where it says, Petkovci, Baljkovica and Memici. Mr. Butler, can you explain how that fits in with the previous combat report that we looked at?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the micro sense, the reflection that they are going back and trying to get the exact line and the exact map line of where that report reflects, and we've discussed this previously. In the larger sense, a confirmation, if you will, that the reports are, in fact, being read and that actions are being taken off of them or certainly that there is an awareness of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, it's Exhibit 675A. The interim combat report at the end of line two specifically refers to Petkovci, Baljkovica and Memici and that was also a report sent to the Drina Corps. Mr. Butler, how credible do you find these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Overall, I find the intercepts relative to the information that's contained in them to be very credible. In a very large number of cases, we've been able to go back off of material from the intercepts, and by virtue of examining the documents that we've seized from the Zvornik Brigade or the Bratunac Brigade, we've been able to go back and validate that what the BiH 2 Corps operators were intercepting, the conversations that they were intercepting were, in many cases, very or directly linked to actions that were happening on the ground and are reflected in other documents. This is one example of that. Clearly, from an analytical perspective of my own view, we received these documents from the BiH government and very candidly, I have to note that one of the first things that I, as an analyst, looked for was to determine whether or not the information that we had received from them was information that was being fed to us for a purpose. So initially, I was very skeptical about this material and I examined it extremely critically with an eye towards finding information that nobody within the BiH government or military could have possibly known or had access to to validate this information. This is one perfect example of how that does occur. This type of intercept couldn't necessarily be manufactured without having knowledge of the 18 July 1995 interim combat report from the Zvornik Brigade which clearly the Muslim government would not have had. Another perfect example of that is the intercepts pertaining to Colonel Popovic, the Assistant Commander for Security, requesting fuel, 500 litres of fuel for the Drina Corps. A very specific amount of fuel, a very specific request, and not only do we see that embodied in the intercepts, but we further see when we look at the Zvornik Brigade technical records, that that fuel was, in fact, dispersed to Colonel Popovic on the days that it was intercepted as doing so. So in a significant number of cases, I am able to validate what the intercept operators heard and information that we received from other sources that, in my mind, there would have been no conceivable way that they would have been aware of otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me ask you though, do you get any sense, from looking at all of these and putting them in the context of other material, of the completeness of it? In other words, we know we certainly don't have all intercepts and some must have been done on secure lines and maybe we didn't get some. But do you get any sense that there might be a whole parallel group of communications that we don't have access to that might change the way in which we construe the ones that we have access to? Or do you get some impression that probably we got all the main lines of communication that were going through?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regards to the telephonic intercepts, these documents, we know -- and I know because we've discussed this issue with the operators on what they were collecting and what they were discarding -- that in that respect, we have everything that they think was militarily relevant. Clearly, there would have been conversations that have occurred that they didn't believe were militarily relevant which may very well be relevant to the criminal aspect of the case. The reality presumption that they didn't know about the context of the crimes as they were occurring and some intercepts that they might have received that would have dealt with that would not have met their criteria for military collection. So in that respect, we don't know. But my overall review of the intercepts is that we probably have the 80 or 90 per cent solution relative to voice intercepts. Relative the other communications, and as discussed, those over secure means, we didn't get those from the BiH government. And in this case, because of the information that we do have, I, as an analyst, have a fairly good understanding of -- I know what I'm missing. Those being certainly the reports from the Drina Corps as well as some from the Main Staff that, because of the way that the material was archived at the Zvornik Brigade and at the Bratunac Brigade, those documents were destroyed years ago. So with respect to the intercepted communications, there are radio teletype messages that are out there that we do not have and some of them that we do not know about, I'm sure. But relative to the voice communications, what I think we have is about the 80 or 90 per cent solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you think from looking at all that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Do you think that it is possible or likely that there could be a lot of orders or commands coming from the top down, from the Drina Corps down that we don't have, to the people in the field?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a possibility, ma'am. I don't see that much of a reflection of it in cases where we have the brigade orders. In many cases, they reference Drina Corps orders that, even though we don't have, we have identification, reference numbers to them. So in that regard, I think I know what I don't know with respect to the orders that were issued. But with respect to other orders that may have come down, that's -- I can only speculate that some certainly did and I'm not aware of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, did you detect, in your analysis, that some intercepted communications were being used to mislead the enemy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly the VRS was fully aware that the voice communications were susceptible to intercept and we know that from previous directives in March and April that there was, in fact, a concerted effort to try to attempt to do that. I looked at that from that perspective and, as an analyst, when one looks at a deception or a potential deception operation, the question becomes what are we trying, we as the people who are launching the deception operation, what are we trying to draw away an enemy's attention from and to? Clearly, in this case, the military objective would have been to try and draw the enemy's attention away from Zepa. The reality was that the entire International Community as well as the BiH and as well as VRS public negotiations were going on, pertaining to Zepa, they could not have realistically hid that fact. The best that they could have potentially done is to mislead or deceive both the International Community and the BiH government as to the strength or the lack of strength of the forces that were attacking Zepa. The counterposition to that is what do you -- what kind of picture does one present to deceive the enemy and to draw their attention? And while there is, in fact, a volume of traffic in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade with the column, the one thing that stands clear on many of these intercepts which do, in fact, discuss criminality is the fact that it would be a very illogical sequence of events to try and deceive an enemy by forwarding traffic related to criminal events which are occurring. That would almost invite additional attention. So looking at all that and given the circumstances on the ground and given the military situation on the ground, and plus the fact that given the combat that is happening in that zone at the time, I just do not see a pattern which would suggest that any of the material being intercepted here by the BiH is the result of some form of a VRS deception operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Butler, in that light, how do you see the fact that there is frequent mention in the communications between several correspondents that this is not a secure means of communication? There is frequent mention in these intercepts that, "We should be careful because we are not communicating along secure lines."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. And under normal conditions, one would expect that those sensitive communications would be passed only via secure means. And when you examine the bulk of the intercepts for the period of, say, an example, July, what you will see is a low level of voice intercepts up to the period of 11 July. You'll see a very high period of intercepts between the period of 12 July to 18 July and then as the situation calms down again, or becomes less dramatic or critical, the information tapers off. What we see is the bulk of the intercepts occurring between the period of 11 July and 18 July, reflective of the significant changing situation in the Corps zone where. Because of the combat activities, because of the continual changing of the plan based on the combat activities and the rapidly changing situations faced by the commanders to have to make decisions, the overriding theme appears to be that because of the speed and because of the necessity to get the information out to the subordinate commanders, that they are willing to sacrifice or set aside their own operational security posture in order to effect a more rapid exchange of information with subordinate or lateral commands. Again, a reflection of the approaching crisis situation that occurs in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade and as that period diminishes, in many cases, you see more of a reflection of less traffic and less sensitive traffic being passed over the open network.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, you mentioned that reports coming into the brigades were destroyed. I just want to clarify. Can you tell us about that, what reports are destroyed and where -- are they completely destroyed or do these reports exist somewhere else, ideally?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one of the very first searches that the Office of the Prosecutor did, which I was a member of, when we searched the headquarters of the Krajina Corps, during that search we had an opportunity to sit down with the Krajina Corps archivist, the person responsible for maintaining the records, and we requested from her an explanation on how the VRS maintains its records. And one of the -- the explanation that we were given was that it is the responsibility of each unit to permanently archive the material that it originates. So in a sense when I say "destroy," it's not a deliberate destruction attempt in order to deceive anybody. What it reflects is that at the end of a year or a two-year period, the units in question, these, the brigades, will go through all of their records, they will bundle up the records and documents that they originated and they will destroy the orders and documents that they did not originate with the knowledge that those will be maintained by the headquarters that originated them. That, of course, is reflected by the documents that we seized, for the most part, from the Bratunac and Zvornik Brigades where we have thousands and thousands of records from those particular brigades but only a few documents from the Drina Corps. Presumably, the Drina Corps would have maintained all of their own documents themselves. So again, not part Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French an English transcripts. of a deliberate destruction attempt, but just a reflection of how the army of the Republika Srpska archives its documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You discussed briefly some of the written orders you've analysed, what kind of oral orders, if any, can we expect, not the kind of orders, but could we expect oral orders to play a role in any kind of a operation, be it a military operation or even a criminal operation? Just briefly, where do oral orders fit into the scheme of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly oral orders fit into the scheme of not only the VRS but of any army. And as we've noted in the previous intercept, General Krstic giving an oral order to his assistant commander to go up to a specific location and to take command and to accomplish a function. How those orders are accounted for is a more formalised process within the VRS. Each command maintains an orders log or journal out of the duty officer's shop, in many cases, and it is his responsibility to notate in that written log, oral orders, who they are received from, the context of those orders. So while certainly the provision is made in the VRS that oral orders are going to be a part of operations and certainly in the context of these operations, the rapidly changing combat, one would expect a lot of orders being given orally as reflected by the intercepts. But they do not remain oral. It's the responsibility of the receiver to note those down in the brigade or in whatever echelon's documents that they have received these oral orders from these individuals and how they are reacting to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to our intercepts of 18 July. The next one is Exhibit 687A and the participants are Krstic and X, who's unidentified. Could you tell us what's happening in the first several lines of this, and then we're going to get to this part where X refers to Krstic as "Chief," we talked about that yesterday, and then I want you to finish up that analysis.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first series of lines, essentially General Krstic asking somebody, was he supposed "to come, up here or there?" Based on the date, presumably we're either talking about does somebody want Krstic to wait in or around Zepa or does he want him to come up to Vlasenica. In this case, it's said: "... the boss said that you should wait for him there in Vlasenica," a reference being that at this point in time, General Krstic is physically located at the Drina Corps headquarters in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And "the boss," whom might that be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this regard, one would think it would be General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, then, shortly after that there's a line that says, "Fuck it ... we pushed them, but it's hard, let me tell you, we didn't have a break." Could that be a discussion about Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I read it, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then X says: "OK chief, OK." Now, have you looked into the translation of "chief," as we discussed yesterday? What word are we talking about here in the B/C/S language?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this regard, we're talking not the word "chief" as in "naccel," normally referred to as Chief of Staff, but we're referring to the more slang version of that, "Dobro, sefe, dobro." "Okay, boss, okay." "Okay, chief, okay." The slang variant, not a specific reference to "chief" as in Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would note that the reference to chief yesterday in another exhibit, that was actually the Chief of Staff word and "Chief" was capitalised by the translation unit. Also, at the bottom of that translation, there's a reference to the "KZ, man" and a problem there. What's that problem that they're having?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A reflection of one of the observations that I noted earlier, that they were having problems in ciphering/securing their communications network, and that as a result of that, you know, they will be able to talk in the secure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to Exhibit 691A. This appears to be a conversation in the evening, the 18th, 2341. Krstic is giving orders to fire at the centre and other things. How does this fit into your analysis, if at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this regard, this is General Krstic giving instructions which I would believe pertain to an artillery fire mission related to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that's going over the open airwaves, but I take it that the artillery round should hit its target before the Muslims have time to transmit this down to Tuzla to get out of the way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, presumably, the theory is that before they can do anything about the information the impact is already made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go now to July 19th intercepts, Exhibit 694, a conversation at 0812 hours. Again, what, if anything, do you make of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, again, a conversation occurring between Colonel Cerovic, the Assistant Commander for Moral, Legal, and Religious Affairs of the VRS Drina Corps -- again, all these figures are circled on the Drina Corps order battle map there -- and Colonel Pandurevic. Discussing the situation, and it's a rather long wrap-up of that situation. They discuss, on the second page, a shift rotation to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and what they're going to do about that, and he notes somewhere down in the middle, on the shift rotation, Cerovic saying: "I'm telling you, the report he sent - there's no way it can be done ... That's Krstic's order, there are no shift rotations until further notice." Again, in this case, General Krstic is noting that in this respect -- you know, he's taking responsibility for the Corps and saying, "We're not doing shift rotations for all the brigades." What is even more significant here is several lines down, Vinko Pandurevic discusses, as a result of casualties and everything else, with Colonel Cerovic, he says: "No, seriously, I've sent you a report yesterday. You could see what kind of losses we sustained." A clear reference to the 18 July 1995 interim combat report. Cerovic, Colonel Cerovic, confirms: "Yes, and I presented that to Krstic and wrote him my own report or a special report based on your interim daily reports." So in this aspect, the Assistant Commander for Moral, Legal, and Religious Affairs of the Drina Corps is confirming to a subordinate brigade commander that "General Krstic," the Corps Commander, "has in fact been presented with your report and he has seen it," as well as his, Colonel Cerovic's, interpretations as to what's going on and what that means. At the end of the day, very much a reflection of the information reporting chain up and down. The final segments are, again, talking about issues of discussions with the duty officer, with Colonel Cerovic making some remarks about one of Colonel Pandurevic's officers that he doesn't see as being up to speed. But those are the primary things that I would pull out of this report. The last piece of information again reflects back to the first page, a reflection as of the time on the 19th, that they're still chasing around, in his words, "150 of them," meaning even at these late dates, the 19th and beyond, elements of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade are still dealing with and encountering significant numbers of Muslims from the long-since-gone column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's 11.00. It's a good time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is a good time for a break. I don't think the transcript was quite correct regarding what I said regarding the timetable for today. The last break will be a ten-minute break, not a 30-minute break, as the interpreters understood me to say. We can't have such long breaks. So we're now going to have a 20-minute break. Then we're going to work from 11.20 on. After, 1.20 until 2.10, a ten-minute break, and then 2.20 until 3.00. I think that is correct now. Yes. A 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, you can continue. We will [as interpreted] have a 25-minute break in the end and not a 20-minute break as I previously indicated. You may now continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Mr. President, what time is the next break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 12.50, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Butler, let's now go on to the 19th, Exhibit 693A. It's the regular combat report from the Zvornik Brigade. Prior to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, sorry to interrupt you but there seems to be a misunderstanding here. I didn't say that we would have a 25-minute break, I said that we had a 25-minute break although I had indicated that there would only be a 20-minute break. Because I can read on the transcript, "We will have a 25-minute break in the end and not a 20-minute break." So that was the reason for your question, and I understand it quite well. It seems that there are some problems with the schedule. I had said that there would be a 20-minute break and not a 25-minute break, which means that we have to be ready after 20 minutes and not 25 minutes. Sorry for this interruption, Mr. McCloskey. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, before getting into the substance of the 19 July Zvornik Brigade combat report, can you briefly summarise for the Court your recollection of who we call the Nezuk survivor, his testimony, because now we're going back into one of our last known crime scenes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Nezuk survivor, as identified, is an individual who is a member of a small group of Muslims who, on about the 18th or 19th of July, were captured by the VRS. A group of those survivors were then subsequently executed by the people who captured them. I believe, if the survivor's accounting is correct, two individuals from the group were held by the VRS and the remaining individuals were shot. The Nezuk survivor in this case was one of the individuals who was shot, in fact survived the summary execution, and later made his way to BiH territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now going to the 19 July combat report, how does the information in that combat report tie in to the factual recitation of the testimony of who we refer to as the Nezuk survivor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this regard, looking at paragraph 2, it discusses during operations that day a story of two Muslim soldiers being captured and 13 being eliminated. Further along the line, it discusses the fact, the presence of the company of the 16th Krajina Brigade. One of the features that the Nezuk -- or one of the instances that the Nezuk survivor recounts is the fact that the soldiers who shot him in the area identified themselves. I believe one of them had a shoulder brassard that said "Krajina." So at a macro level, you could look at this incident they're discussing here and it's a very similar story to that which the Nezuk survivor tells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Geographically, my recollection is Nezuk may not have been extremely precise, but is this roughly the same geographic area noted in this report as -- is it the same as that recounted by the Nezuk survivor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What else, if anything, do you get from this report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the broader level, a recognition that the Zvornik Infantry Brigade is still coming across prisoners -- or, I'm sorry, Muslim men in zone and is conducting combat operations in relation to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I note at the bottom of the page that one Serb soldier, Nenad Asentic, was wounded and Milenko Milosevic was killed. So what does that tell you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, a reflection of armed combat occurring.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to intercept 696A. What, if anything, do you get out of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, a conversation between General Krstic and an individual named Milankovic whom I do not know. Broadly, all I really get out of this conversation is the fact that General Krstic is still discussing things, issues over the telephone network and is aware of what's going on in a broad sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to Exhibit 698A, 19 July conversation, 2157 hours between Krstic and Jevdevic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, we're certainly discussing the tactical situation as it's occurring in the zone of the Corps. Jevdevic, then Major Jevdevic the Commander of the 5th Communications Battalion of the Drina Corps, an individual identified as Jokic, maybe Major Jokic of the Zvornik Brigade but in this context, I don't believe so. Talking about having checked with the commanders. One of the guys identified Trivic, who would be Colonel Trivic in this case, the Commander of the 2nd Romanija Brigade. Srna or Blagojevic, in this case, Blagojevic being the Commander of the Bratunac Brigade. They are talking about 200 men on the buses. This corresponds with the reinforcements that are coming into the Zepa area for intervention where needed, and Krstic is passing the orders that he needs an additional 200 men, not drivers, but 200 soldiers with weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Has the investigation revealed anything about the person Srna, this person identified as Srna?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they have developed some information but it escapes my memory at this point what Srna is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anything aside from this conversation that you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, a reflection that General Krstic is in communication with members of the Drina Corps pertaining to military activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, I would note that that is -- closes one main chapter of the case and we'll go on to some other documents that are related which is Exhibit 701. But before we get to those documents, Mr. Butler, those are documents that were recovered from, I believe, the Bratunac Brigade. Can you tell us, briefly, about some of these documents that were recovered from the Bratunac Brigade and just briefly what they reflect. I don't think we'll need to go through them each individually.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the OTP conducted a search of the Bratunac Brigade, one of the offices searched was the office of the former Chief of Security, then Captain First Class Momir Nikolic. Documents seized in that office included handwritten notes which, when the notes are reviewed, indicate that they are the results of field interrogations of select Muslim individuals who were, for whatever reason or point in time, in the custody of the VRS, were questioned and information extracted from them. Taking these names and then reviewing them against the ICRC missing list, it's revealed that these individuals are on the missing list as missing from Srebrenica. And looking at the missing list in most cases, the names of the missing were last seen alive on the 12th and 13th in geographic locations that correspond with the location and zone of the Bratunac infantry Brigade. So while these interrogation notes are not dated, when you look at the notes and you read the information extracted, clearly the trend that whoever is doing the interrogations, they are looking for information as to the names and the locations of significant identified Muslim leaders who are part of the column, where people believe that they are to be, and what their intentions are. So again, at the broader level, these documents indicate that, for whatever reason, certainly a small number of individuals who were part of that large process of prisoners being taken, surrendering from the column in the zone of the Bratunac, at least some of them were formally talked to in the form of an interrogation. Information was extracted from them, demonstrating that they are in the proper custody of the army of the Republika Srpska in general, and the Bratunac Brigade in particular, and then now these people are listed as missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would briefly call Your Honours' attention to the testimony of Helge Brunborg where he referred to that many names in Bosnia are similar and the key identifier is, many times, the father's name of the individual as well, of course, the date of birth. Mr. Butler, do most of these documents, and let's start with Exhibit 701, actually provide enough information to get a good identification from the ICRC missing list?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly in this case: Last name, first name, father's name, date of birth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what in these notes ties it to the -- to our situation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last line in the notation, "a number of people wish to break through to the Drina to surrender to Serbia."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we haven't heard much about people making it over to Serbia and I don't intend to go into that in great length, but did some people actually -- some of the Muslim refugees make it over to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that some did but I'm not familiar with the numbers or circumstances behind that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let's go to the next exhibit, 702A. Just again, lists of individuals with identifying information noting that they crossed over to Cerska with the first group, the mention of a column. Going over to Exhibit 703A, this exhibit also indicates from the notes information that is relevant to the analysis, things that we'd known about or heard about related to this case.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now Exhibit 704A, that's a similar sort of set of notes with similar information. And going over to Exhibit 705A, can you tell us what this work represents in this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular exhibit, which is an extract from the narrative, reflects the names of the individuals listed and where they were cross-checked against the International Committee for the Red Cross missing list registration number, and where they were last seen alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And before we get to the next chapter, there's something I wanted to go back to; this morning's discussion of intercepts, very briefly. In terms of the numbers of -- or the intercepts that the Court has been provided, are you aware of the process that there were other intercepts on the same dates involving conversations that were not brought forward to the Court?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there were some.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And roughly why was that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those conversations represent low-level -- we call them tactical radio communications between various elements of the Zvornik Brigade related to the combat functions. One of the other aspects of intercepts that the Bosnian Muslims were doing was not only with the intercepting the large radio telephone networks, the radio telephone communication one, but also the tactical radio intercepts, in some cases, the small portable radios, in some cases the low-level VHF radios between companies and battalion commands. This communication which we have, at this level, they were very strict about following communication security. They used a lot of code words and call signs, and most of the information that we can derive from it is relative to combat operations. And so while it represents an aspect of the combat operations that are occurring, the information derived from it has no relative bearing on the larger scale operations of the Drina Corps. Again, while that information was reviewed, in my analysis, I did not deem it to be relevant to the material and the issues that I discussed as part of the narrative and as part of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you have talked about notations of prisoners in the Bratunac Brigade for our time period and the next series of exhibits, beginning with Exhibit 706, involves prisoners captured in the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility during this time period. Can you brief the Court on what your analysis has done in regard to those prisoners and how you've tied it into the testimony of the older Branjevo Farm survivor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regards to the prisoners in the area of the Zvornik Brigade, there are two distinct groupings. The first grouping, as we have alluded to with the Nezuk survivor, were those prisoners who were taken as part of a column. And in many cases, where a few of them were kept and a number of them were subsummarily [sic] executed. Another set of prisoners and in one particular case, a well-documented one, is a group of Muslims who, on analysis, appear to be survivors from a mass execution up at the Branjevo Military Farm who escaped from that execution and who, several days later, came back into the custody of the VRS and then were subsequently executed. So in that regard with the Zvornik Brigade prisoners, those are the two classifications that we have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the Zvornik Brigade prisoners were executed, they were, in fact, on the -- found to be missing from the ICRC list; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I presume that they didn't have an accidental death or some other. All right. Let's -- can you tell the Court the -- about the documents, what do the documents tell about the story of those particular prisoners, how many of them were there and what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, the situation in question arises from two soldiers of the 1st Battalion of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade who are charged by the brigade command, specifically the Assistant Commander for Security, Lieutenant Drago Nikolic for charges relating to aiding and abetting the enemy. They are accused of providing aid in comfort, for lack of a better word, to four Muslim prisoners who were trying to escape the custody of the VRS. What we have in a series of documents that reflects the legal proceedings that were initiated against these two Zvornik Brigade soldiers. Part of those proceedings include signed witness statements from the four Muslim prisoners who they were accused of helping. These four Muslim prisoners are now on the ICRC missing list. Further, when you take that series of events and compare it to one of the survivor accounts of the Branjevo Military Farm survivors, he notes that there were a group of four individuals who also had escaped, and he recognises one of them or he remembers one from a specific village that he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French an English transcripts. grew up in. And of these four individuals, one of them as listed on the witness statement taken in his name is that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the village?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look in the actual exhibit. I don't remember it offhand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Something like Jagonje?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the story that is told by the statements in the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What this story tells is that these four individuals departing from the area of Srebrenica essentially tried to escape through the Nezuk area, did not escape through the Nezuk area and, if I may go to the map here for a second, took a route from the Nezuk area laterally across the entire front area of the Zvornik Brigade with the intention of breaking out in this area to the north towards a Muslim military facility known as roughly Teoack. T-e-o-a-c-k, I believe it's spelled. As we've been able to indicate through the records and documents, the overwhelming majority of the column went out in this broad area here, yet these four individuals, according to their statements, made a trek throughout the entire zone of the Zvornik Brigade to try and get out in this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we just for one second go to another exhibit that I think will illustrate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
